romania.title: Misiune medicală rară în România: Cum i-a fost salvată viața unei tinere care a fost transportată cu sângele oxigenat în afara corpului
romania.summary: O misiune medicală rară i-a salvat viața unei adolescente de 18 ani, aflate la doar câteva ore de un deznodământ dramatic. Miruna avea plămânii grav afectați de o infecție, iar singura ei șansă a fost ECMO, un aparat care oxigenează sângele în afara corpului și preia temporar funcția plămânilor. O echipă de la Spitalul Floreasca a plecat în urmă cu o lună în toiul nopții la Craiova, a conectat-o la aparat și a adus-o cu elicopterul la București. A fost primul transfer aeromedical pe suport ECMO realizat de medicii de la Floreasca. Astăzi adolescenta este bine și spune că vrea să devină medic.

medical.title: WHO declares Uganda Ebola-free
medical.summary: Uganda was declared officially Ebola-free by the World Health Organization on Thursday after 42 days without a new case.

medical.title: Special aspherical glasses slow down childhood myopia progression, two-year trial finds
medical.summary: The number of people who need prescription glasses to correct their vision is increasing each year as nearsightedness, or myopia, becomes more common worldwide. Current projections suggest cases could reach 50% by 2050, affecting nearly 5 billion people.

medical.title: How public safety can influence public health
medical.summary: A basketball court, soccer field or playground may help make a park inviting. But a new UC Irvine study suggests that the way public safety is approached can also influence how people use those spaces.

medical.title: No safe tan: Why Canada's sunburn problem keeps getting worse
medical.summary: Scroll through social media and you will encounter a strange vocabulary for an old impulse: "tanmaxxing," "UV chasing" and "SPF shunning." In some corners of the internet, sunscreen is described as toxic, while a "natural" tan is portrayed as protective.

medical.title: Eating more ultra-processed foods may raise prostate cancer risk by 30%
medical.summary: Ultra-processed foods make up a huge share of the American diet, and new research suggests they may carry another serious health risk for men. In a nationally representative study of more than 17,000 U.S. men, those who ate more ultra-processed foods, including soft drinks, packaged snacks, cereals, and processed meats, had roughly 24% to 31% higher risks of prostate cancer after accounting for factors such as age, smoking, race and ethnicity, and poverty status.

medical.title: Study finds gaps in home rehab after joint replacement
medical.summary: Every year, hundreds of thousands of older Americans recover from hip and knee replacement surgery at home. For many, that recovery depends on timely access to physical or occupational therapy after leaving the hospital.

medical.title: New approach to mental health care reduces hospital admissions
medical.summary: A new approach to caring for people experiencing a mental health crisis, emphasizing continuity and community, can reduce hospital admissions and improve satisfaction with care, a study led by a University College London (UCL) researcher found.

medical.title: Stroke rehab should start early and address physical, cognitive and mental health
medical.summary: A stroke can change life in an instant, affecting everything from walking and speaking to memory, mood and the ability to perform everyday tasks. Recovery often continues for months or even years as survivors of stroke work to regain independence and quality of life. A new guideline from the American Stroke Association, a division of the American Heart Association, emphasizes that every person who has a stroke should receive a personalized assessment and begin rehabilitation during their hospital stay once they are medically stable, supported by a team of specialists who can address physical, cognitive, communication and emotional challenges throughout recovery. The 2026 Guideline for Adult Stroke Rehabilitation and Recovery was published today in the journal Stroke.

medical.title: Life after: oil
medical.summary: Former oil executive Samantha Cooper once helped power the industry. Now she’s fighting to end its hold on our future The post Life after: oil appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: Scientists discover a brain “brake” that can shut down chronic pain
medical.summary: Researchers discovered a brain-based “brake” that can shut down chronic nerve pain in mice by calming an overactive pain circuit. Targeting this system more precisely could one day lead to powerful pain relief without affecting opioid receptors throughout the entire body.

medical.title: New start-up aims to cut cost of producing proteins for cancer care and diagnostics
medical.summary: A new University of Kent start-up has been launched to commercialize biotechnology that could make it cheaper and easier to produce proteins used in cancer treatments, vaccines and diagnostic tests. Sirius Proteins was registered this month, taking technology developed and patented at Kent a step closer to wider commercial use.

medical.title: What went right this week: a ‘pivotal moment’ for cancer research, plus more
medical.summary: A ‘pivotal moment’ for cancer treatment, resurgent whales, and the city that made public transport free, plus more The post What went right this week: a ‘pivotal moment’ for cancer research, plus more appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: ‘We like breaking the rules’: the radical farm that yields results
medical.summary: An Italian farm that plays annoying sounds to pests and leans in to quantum physics is getting surprising results The post ‘We like breaking the rules’: the radical farm that yields results appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years — the screen time result was unexpected
medical.summary: An eight-year Finnish study found that children who spent more time on screens tended to show better cognitive processing as teenagers, challenging common assumptions about screen use. Researchers say the key may be balancing physical activity with screen activities that encourage learning, creativity, and active thinking.

medical.title: A little-known protein may be fueling Alzheimer’s — and scientists found a way to block it
medical.summary: An experimental Alzheimer’s compound prevented damaging protein clumps from forming in the brains of mice, helping nerve cells survive longer and reducing amyloid buildup. The treatment also appeared to improve heart health and slow some signs of aging, raising hopes for an entirely new way to combat dementia.

science.title: AI searched 100 million possibilities and found a cheaper way to 3D-print a NASA rocket alloy
science.summary: Researchers used AI to search through more than 100 million possible settings for 3D-printing a high-performance NASA alloy. After only 40 experiments, the system identified six successful configurations, including one that worked at a record-low 500 watts. That could allow GRCop-42, currently difficult and expensive to print, to be made with much more widely available equipment.

science.title: AI helps uncover oyster DNA changes linked to climate resilience
science.summary: While a colleague traveled along the East Coast from Canada to the Gulf of Mexico collecting oysters, Northeastern University bioinformatics graduate student Megha Prasad worked away at her computer. She zeroed in on DNA, the molecule containing instructions for making proteins that shape the critters' traits. It also holds the key to their adaptation to the changing climate.

science.title: Venus's mysterious clouds may hide an exceptionally strong light absorber
science.summary: Venus appears pale yellow in visible light, but ultraviolet images reveal dramatic dark and bright patterns moving with the planet's upper sulfuric acid clouds. Scientists have known about these markings for roughly a century, yet the chemical identity of the material responsible—the "unknown absorber"—remains unresolved.

science.title: “I jumped from my chair” – Astronomers spot Betelgeuse’s hidden companion
science.summary: Astronomers have captured their clearest image yet of Betelgeuse’s long-suspected companion, potentially ending a search that lasted about 100 years. The surprisingly massive hidden star could help explain Betelgeuse’s changing brightness and may influence its future supernova.

science.title: New clues about how space travel may affect women's health
science.summary: As space missions become longer and ambitions for deep-space travel grow, scientists are working to understand how life beyond Earth may affect every system in the human body. Two years after her initial study took flight, Begum Mathyk, MD, and collaborators are continuing to push the frontier of women's health in space, this time by examining how altered gravity may affect female biology.

science.title: School phone bans are working in Toronto elementary schools—and failing in high schools
science.summary: Concerns that phones and social media are harming student learning and youth mental health have pushed school systems across Canada and the United States to restrict student phone use.

science.title: Tomatoes get flavor boost from green bin compost
science.summary: Commercially farmed tomatoes taste sweeter when food and garden waste compost is added to their soil, a University of Queensland study has found. Researchers in the School of Agriculture and Food Sustainability grew tomatoes in southeast Queensland with and without the compost and put the resulting crops through chemical and sensory analysis.

science.title: Geomimicry offers a new framework for engineering sustainable materials
science.summary: When engineers look to nature for inspiration, they often turn to living systems. The flight of birds has influenced aircraft design, gecko feet inspired new adhesives and lotus leaves led to the development of self-cleaning surfaces.

science.title: Two decades of fieldwork produce the first complete guide to the native reptiles of the Turks and Caicos Islands
science.summary: A researcher from the University of North Carolina Asheville has published the first comprehensive checklist of the native terrestrial reptiles of the Turks and Caicos Islands (TCI), drawing on 20 years of collaborative fieldwork to create a single illustrated reference for scientists, conservationists and nature enthusiasts.

science.title: Species discoveries reveal emerging biodiversity hotspots worldwide
science.summary: We share our planet with millions of plants and animals. This variety of life is known as biodiversity, a term encompassing everything from microscopic genes to entire ecosystems, such as deserts and vibrant coral reefs.

science.title: Your dislike of eating bugs may be 9,000 years old
science.summary: Ancient teeth and human DNA are revealing a surprising history of insect eating. Modern humans in northern Eurasia appear to have eaten insects only occasionally, while Neanderthals may have consumed them much more regularly. Populations near the tropics also retained genes that make insect exoskeletons easier to digest.

science.title: Does envy influences the way we vote?
science.summary: Envy plays a greater role when resources are allocated through majority voting than when we make decisions individually. This is shown by new research from Linköping University, Sweden. According to the researchers, the explanation may be that our sense of personal responsibility diminishes when an individual vote is unlikely to determine the outcome.

science.title: Going beyond simple models of neural networks: Extended mean-field theory offers a better approach
science.summary: Physics is most readily applied to relatively simple systems: a pendulum, two electrons colliding or the structure of the solar system. But when systems become complicated—when many particles interact with one another, in condensed matter systems such as gases and fluids or in the cosmology of the early universe—simplifications can be made using a technique called classical or extended mean-field theory.

science.title: Expert Q&A: How blended finance can help Canadian communities unlock capital for impact
science.summary: Blended Finance Canada is a joint initiative between the University of Victoria's (UVic) Impact Investing Hub, a division of Accelerating Community Energy Transformation (ACET), Scale Institute and Spring to develop a knowledge hub offering practical guidance to help communities across Canada understand and use blended finance to overcome funding barriers.

science.title: A mysterious cosmic hum may come from 13-billion-year-old dark stars
science.summary: Today’s mysterious gravitational-wave background may preserve clues about how the Universe’s first supermassive black holes formed. Descendants of hypothetical Dark Stars could be responsible for a major portion of the signal, offering a surprising new way to investigate cosmic dawn and dark matter.

science.title: Scientists switch on a strange new form of magnetism in an ultrathin material
science.summary: Scientists have found a surprising way to potentially switch on an unusual form of magnetism in ruthenium dioxide, a material that normally appears nonmagnetic. When the material was made into an ultrathin film only a few atomic layers thick and placed under strain, its electrons developed patterns consistent with altermagnetism, a recently proposed magnetic state with promising uses in advanced electronics.

science.title: Climate change leaves its mark on America's largest reservoir
science.summary: From high in the hills around Las Vegas, tourist Choune Osterero gazes down at the line of chalky mineral deposits left on the rocks around Lake Mead as the level of America's largest reservoir has dropped over the last quarter-century of drought.

science.title: Fleeting sugar pairs may help curb abnormal cell-growth signals
science.summary: Acting as armor, a scaffold and a communication platform in one, our cells' plasma membrane lies at the heart of many crucial cellular processes. Traditionally, it has been thought to function through interactions among its various proteins and lipids. Now, researchers have revealed a crucial yet often overlooked membrane component—complex sugar chains, known as glycans, carried by certain membrane lipids called gangliosides and many membrane proteins.

science.title: Heat makes emergency rooms busier. Study shows which illness and injuries rise during hot spells
science.summary: When the temperature heats up, so do emergency rooms, according to a massive study of Chicago hospital and urgent care records, which found increased accidental gunshot wounds, kidney complaints, skin problems, varicose veins and even mental health issues related to marijuana use.

science.title: Light particles reveal critical scaling in a two-dimensional photon gas
science.summary: A team of researchers from the University of Bonn, Heidelberg University and the National Autonomous University of Mexico has studied the critical behavior of light particles (photons) close to a phase transition. This critical scaling behavior, which sees thermodynamic quantities grow extremely large or diverge shortly prior to Bose-Einstein condensation, had never before been seen in photon gases until the researchers successfully secured precisely this proof.

science.title: How to keep your child's tablets, laptops from becoming distractions from schoolwork
science.summary: Tablets and computers have become crucial school supplies for many students. But the same devices children use to read text, write essays, solve math problems or research history projects can also offer distractions in the form of games, social media and web browsing.

science.title: Virtual cell model could accelerate protein-degrader therapy design
science.summary: A team of Weill Cornell Medicine investigators has developed a computer model that will help scientists more efficiently develop protein-destroying therapies, a newer type of treatment that is particularly promising for cancer. The study is published July 13 in Nature Communications.

science.title: 324-million-year-old fossil reveals how insects conquered land
science.summary: Ancient fossils suggest insects conquered land through a long amphibious phase rather than making an abrupt jump from water to dry ground. A newly identified 324-million-year-old species still carried paddle-like abdominal limbs, revealing an evolutionary bridge between aquatic ancestors and modern six-legged insects.

science.summary: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 August 27 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Colorful Aurora over […]

science.title: Some Galápagos 'yellow' sea turtles remain homebodies, surprising scientists
science.summary: Sea turtles are famous for being prodigious wanderers. Guided by Earth's magnetic field, ocean currents and the sun, they tend to crisscross the seas in search of food, returning to the region of their birth every few years to breed. So when scientists discovered a population of sea turtles that appear to be very much homebodies, they were taken aback.

environment.title: Cambodia defies UN call to free ‘arbitrarily jailed’ environmental activists
environment.summary: CHIANG MAI, Thailand — The Cambodian government has defended its continued imprisonment of five environmental activists, after the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention declared the five had been arbitrarily detained and called for their immediate release. The activists, from environmental group Mother Nature Cambodia, have since 2024 been serving prison sentences of between […]

environment.title: In Java’s hills, former bird hunters are rebuilding a songbird haven
environment.summary: PURWOREJO, Indonesia — As a young man, Parman hunted songbirds here in the Menoreh Hills, a landscape of karst valleys near the Indonesian city of Yogyakarta. The area is now a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, but back then Parman would raid nests for rare birds, taking fledglings before they had learned to fly, then raising them […]

environment.title: A ‘leading’ Chinese miner of Mozambique’s heavy sands linked to environmental destruction
environment.summary: A sand mining operation along the coast of central Mozambique’s Zambezia Province decimated hundreds of hectares of mangroves in just a few years, a Mongabay investigation has found. The area is under the control of Mozambique Heavy Sand Company VIII, part-owned by the Jinan Yuxiao Group, an influential Chinese mining group claiming to hold more than […]

environment.title: A Sumatran villager lost ground to the sea. So he planted mangroves
environment.summary: In a coastal village on the Indonesian island of Sumatra, an oil palm and pineapple grower named Harisyah is fighting rapid coastal erosion. The region’s northern coastline, which sits on carbon-rich tropical peat soils, is losing ground to the sea at a rate of more than 6 meters (20 feet) annually. Researchers attribute the retreat […]

environment.title: China’s Tianmu Mountain reserve tackles modern conservation amid religious tradition
environment.summary: Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian traditions have long guided the protection of plants and wildlife in a nature reserve on Tianmu Mountain in eastern China. Local temples enforced strict rules and punishments against forest destruction, but, following the reserve’s recent expansion, state regulations now provide the formal legal framework for the area. Local officials say religious […]

environment.source: NASA Earth Observatory - Image of the Day
environment.title: Rare, Widespread Snow in the Atacama Desert
environment.summary: Back-to-back winter storms in August 2026 brought snowfall to northern Chile, from the Andes to near the Pacific coast. The post Rare, Widespread Snow in the Atacama Desert appeared first on NASA Science .

environment.title: Animals have been eating nature’s original bioplastic for millions of years
environment.summary: Nature invented biodegradable plastic long before humans did—and animals may have been feeding on it for hundreds of millions of years. Researchers discovered that dozens of animal species possess enzymes capable of breaking down microbial bioplastics called PHAs, a talent once thought to belong only to microorganisms.

environment.title: Chasing Fire Clouds in Utah
environment.summary: NASA aircraft are sampling smoke lofted high into the atmosphere by one of the most formidable cloud types in the sky—towering, smoke-infused pyrocumulonimbus. The post Chasing Fire Clouds in Utah appeared first on NASA Science .

mix_items.title: “I jumped from my chair” – Astronomers spot Betelgeuse’s hidden companion
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have captured their clearest image yet of Betelgeuse’s long-suspected companion, potentially ending a search that lasted about 100 years. The surprisingly massive hidden star could help explain Betelgeuse’s changing brightness and may influence its future supernova.

mix_items.title: No safe tan: Why Canada's sunburn problem keeps getting worse
mix_items.summary: Scroll through social media and you will encounter a strange vocabulary for an old impulse: "tanmaxxing," "UV chasing" and "SPF shunning." In some corners of the internet, sunscreen is described as toxic, while a "natural" tan is portrayed as protective.

mix_items.title: New clues about how space travel may affect women's health
mix_items.summary: As space missions become longer and ambitions for deep-space travel grow, scientists are working to understand how life beyond Earth may affect every system in the human body. Two years after her initial study took flight, Begum Mathyk, MD, and collaborators are continuing to push the frontier of women's health in space, this time by examining how altered gravity may affect female biology.

mix_items.title: School phone bans are working in Toronto elementary schools—and failing in high schools
mix_items.summary: Concerns that phones and social media are harming student learning and youth mental health have pushed school systems across Canada and the United States to restrict student phone use.

mix_items.title: Tomatoes get flavor boost from green bin compost
mix_items.summary: Commercially farmed tomatoes taste sweeter when food and garden waste compost is added to their soil, a University of Queensland study has found. Researchers in the School of Agriculture and Food Sustainability grew tomatoes in southeast Queensland with and without the compost and put the resulting crops through chemical and sensory analysis.

mix_items.title: Geomimicry offers a new framework for engineering sustainable materials
mix_items.summary: When engineers look to nature for inspiration, they often turn to living systems. The flight of birds has influenced aircraft design, gecko feet inspired new adhesives and lotus leaves led to the development of self-cleaning surfaces.

mix_items.title: Two decades of fieldwork produce the first complete guide to the native reptiles of the Turks and Caicos Islands
mix_items.summary: A researcher from the University of North Carolina Asheville has published the first comprehensive checklist of the native terrestrial reptiles of the Turks and Caicos Islands (TCI), drawing on 20 years of collaborative fieldwork to create a single illustrated reference for scientists, conservationists and nature enthusiasts.

mix_items.title: Species discoveries reveal emerging biodiversity hotspots worldwide
mix_items.summary: We share our planet with millions of plants and animals. This variety of life is known as biodiversity, a term encompassing everything from microscopic genes to entire ecosystems, such as deserts and vibrant coral reefs.

mix_items.title: Your dislike of eating bugs may be 9,000 years old
mix_items.summary: Ancient teeth and human DNA are revealing a surprising history of insect eating. Modern humans in northern Eurasia appear to have eaten insects only occasionally, while Neanderthals may have consumed them much more regularly. Populations near the tropics also retained genes that make insect exoskeletons easier to digest.

mix_items.title: Eating more ultra-processed foods may raise prostate cancer risk by 30%
mix_items.summary: Ultra-processed foods make up a huge share of the American diet, and new research suggests they may carry another serious health risk for men. In a nationally representative study of more than 17,000 U.S. men, those who ate more ultra-processed foods, including soft drinks, packaged snacks, cereals, and processed meats, had roughly 24% to 31% higher risks of prostate cancer after accounting for factors such as age, smoking, race and ethnicity, and poverty status.

mix_items.title: Study finds gaps in home rehab after joint replacement
mix_items.summary: Every year, hundreds of thousands of older Americans recover from hip and knee replacement surgery at home. For many, that recovery depends on timely access to physical or occupational therapy after leaving the hospital.

mix_items.title: Does envy influences the way we vote?
mix_items.summary: Envy plays a greater role when resources are allocated through majority voting than when we make decisions individually. This is shown by new research from Linköping University, Sweden. According to the researchers, the explanation may be that our sense of personal responsibility diminishes when an individual vote is unlikely to determine the outcome.

mix_items.title: Going beyond simple models of neural networks: Extended mean-field theory offers a better approach
mix_items.summary: Physics is most readily applied to relatively simple systems: a pendulum, two electrons colliding or the structure of the solar system. But when systems become complicated—when many particles interact with one another, in condensed matter systems such as gases and fluids or in the cosmology of the early universe—simplifications can be made using a technique called classical or extended mean-field theory.

mix_items.title: New approach to mental health care reduces hospital admissions
mix_items.summary: A new approach to caring for people experiencing a mental health crisis, emphasizing continuity and community, can reduce hospital admissions and improve satisfaction with care, a study led by a University College London (UCL) researcher found.

mix_items.title: Expert Q&A: How blended finance can help Canadian communities unlock capital for impact
mix_items.summary: Blended Finance Canada is a joint initiative between the University of Victoria's (UVic) Impact Investing Hub, a division of Accelerating Community Energy Transformation (ACET), Scale Institute and Spring to develop a knowledge hub offering practical guidance to help communities across Canada understand and use blended finance to overcome funding barriers.

mix_items.title: Cambodia defies UN call to free ‘arbitrarily jailed’ environmental activists
mix_items.summary: CHIANG MAI, Thailand — The Cambodian government has defended its continued imprisonment of five environmental activists, after the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention declared the five had been arbitrarily detained and called for their immediate release. The activists, from environmental group Mother Nature Cambodia, have since 2024 been serving prison sentences of between […]

mix_items.title: In Java’s hills, former bird hunters are rebuilding a songbird haven
mix_items.summary: PURWOREJO, Indonesia — As a young man, Parman hunted songbirds here in the Menoreh Hills, a landscape of karst valleys near the Indonesian city of Yogyakarta. The area is now a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, but back then Parman would raid nests for rare birds, taking fledglings before they had learned to fly, then raising them […]

mix_items.title: A mysterious cosmic hum may come from 13-billion-year-old dark stars
mix_items.summary: Today’s mysterious gravitational-wave background may preserve clues about how the Universe’s first supermassive black holes formed. Descendants of hypothetical Dark Stars could be responsible for a major portion of the signal, offering a surprising new way to investigate cosmic dawn and dark matter.

mix_items.title: Scientists switch on a strange new form of magnetism in an ultrathin material
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found a surprising way to potentially switch on an unusual form of magnetism in ruthenium dioxide, a material that normally appears nonmagnetic. When the material was made into an ultrathin film only a few atomic layers thick and placed under strain, its electrons developed patterns consistent with altermagnetism, a recently proposed magnetic state with promising uses in advanced electronics.

mix_items.title: Climate change leaves its mark on America's largest reservoir
mix_items.summary: From high in the hills around Las Vegas, tourist Choune Osterero gazes down at the line of chalky mineral deposits left on the rocks around Lake Mead as the level of America's largest reservoir has dropped over the last quarter-century of drought.

mix_items.title: Stroke rehab should start early and address physical, cognitive and mental health
mix_items.summary: A stroke can change life in an instant, affecting everything from walking and speaking to memory, mood and the ability to perform everyday tasks. Recovery often continues for months or even years as survivors of stroke work to regain independence and quality of life. A new guideline from the American Stroke Association, a division of the American Heart Association, emphasizes that every person who has a stroke should receive a personalized assessment and begin rehabilitation during their hospital stay once they are medically stable, supported by a team of specialists who can address physical, cognitive, communication and emotional challenges throughout recovery. The 2026 Guideline for Adult Stroke Rehabilitation and Recovery was published today in the journal Stroke.

mix_items.title: Fleeting sugar pairs may help curb abnormal cell-growth signals
mix_items.summary: Acting as armor, a scaffold and a communication platform in one, our cells' plasma membrane lies at the heart of many crucial cellular processes. Traditionally, it has been thought to function through interactions among its various proteins and lipids. Now, researchers have revealed a crucial yet often overlooked membrane component—complex sugar chains, known as glycans, carried by certain membrane lipids called gangliosides and many membrane proteins.

mix_items.title: Heat makes emergency rooms busier. Study shows which illness and injuries rise during hot spells
mix_items.summary: When the temperature heats up, so do emergency rooms, according to a massive study of Chicago hospital and urgent care records, which found increased accidental gunshot wounds, kidney complaints, skin problems, varicose veins and even mental health issues related to marijuana use.

mix_items.title: A ‘leading’ Chinese miner of Mozambique’s heavy sands linked to environmental destruction
mix_items.summary: A sand mining operation along the coast of central Mozambique’s Zambezia Province decimated hundreds of hectares of mangroves in just a few years, a Mongabay investigation has found. The area is under the control of Mozambique Heavy Sand Company VIII, part-owned by the Jinan Yuxiao Group, an influential Chinese mining group claiming to hold more than […]

mix_items.title: Light particles reveal critical scaling in a two-dimensional photon gas
mix_items.summary: A team of researchers from the University of Bonn, Heidelberg University and the National Autonomous University of Mexico has studied the critical behavior of light particles (photons) close to a phase transition. This critical scaling behavior, which sees thermodynamic quantities grow extremely large or diverge shortly prior to Bose-Einstein condensation, had never before been seen in photon gases until the researchers successfully secured precisely this proof.

mix_items.title: A Sumatran villager lost ground to the sea. So he planted mangroves
mix_items.summary: In a coastal village on the Indonesian island of Sumatra, an oil palm and pineapple grower named Harisyah is fighting rapid coastal erosion. The region’s northern coastline, which sits on carbon-rich tropical peat soils, is losing ground to the sea at a rate of more than 6 meters (20 feet) annually. Researchers attribute the retreat […]

mix_items.title: How to keep your child's tablets, laptops from becoming distractions from schoolwork
mix_items.summary: Tablets and computers have become crucial school supplies for many students. But the same devices children use to read text, write essays, solve math problems or research history projects can also offer distractions in the form of games, social media and web browsing.

mix_items.title: Virtual cell model could accelerate protein-degrader therapy design
mix_items.summary: A team of Weill Cornell Medicine investigators has developed a computer model that will help scientists more efficiently develop protein-destroying therapies, a newer type of treatment that is particularly promising for cancer. The study is published July 13 in Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: 324-million-year-old fossil reveals how insects conquered land
mix_items.summary: Ancient fossils suggest insects conquered land through a long amphibious phase rather than making an abrupt jump from water to dry ground. A newly identified 324-million-year-old species still carried paddle-like abdominal limbs, revealing an evolutionary bridge between aquatic ancestors and modern six-legged insects.

mix_items.title: Life after: oil
mix_items.summary: Former oil executive Samantha Cooper once helped power the industry. Now she’s fighting to end its hold on our future The post Life after: oil appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a brain “brake” that can shut down chronic pain
mix_items.summary: Researchers discovered a brain-based “brake” that can shut down chronic nerve pain in mice by calming an overactive pain circuit. Targeting this system more precisely could one day lead to powerful pain relief without affecting opioid receptors throughout the entire body.

mix_items.title: China’s Tianmu Mountain reserve tackles modern conservation amid religious tradition
mix_items.summary: Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian traditions have long guided the protection of plants and wildlife in a nature reserve on Tianmu Mountain in eastern China. Local temples enforced strict rules and punishments against forest destruction, but, following the reserve’s recent expansion, state regulations now provide the formal legal framework for the area. Local officials say religious […]

mix_items.title: Some Galápagos 'yellow' sea turtles remain homebodies, surprising scientists
mix_items.summary: Sea turtles are famous for being prodigious wanderers. Guided by Earth's magnetic field, ocean currents and the sun, they tend to crisscross the seas in search of food, returning to the region of their birth every few years to breed. So when scientists discovered a population of sea turtles that appear to be very much homebodies, they were taken aback.

mix_items.title: Rare, Widespread Snow in the Atacama Desert
mix_items.summary: Back-to-back winter storms in August 2026 brought snowfall to northern Chile, from the Andes to near the Pacific coast. The post Rare, Widespread Snow in the Atacama Desert appeared first on NASA Science .

mix_items.title: New start-up aims to cut cost of producing proteins for cancer care and diagnostics
mix_items.summary: A new University of Kent start-up has been launched to commercialize biotechnology that could make it cheaper and easier to produce proteins used in cancer treatments, vaccines and diagnostic tests. Sirius Proteins was registered this month, taking technology developed and patented at Kent a step closer to wider commercial use.

mix_items.title: What went right this week: a ‘pivotal moment’ for cancer research, plus more
mix_items.summary: A ‘pivotal moment’ for cancer treatment, resurgent whales, and the city that made public transport free, plus more The post What went right this week: a ‘pivotal moment’ for cancer research, plus more appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: ‘We like breaking the rules’: the radical farm that yields results
mix_items.summary: An Italian farm that plays annoying sounds to pests and leans in to quantum physics is getting surprising results The post ‘We like breaking the rules’: the radical farm that yields results appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years — the screen time result was unexpected
mix_items.summary: An eight-year Finnish study found that children who spent more time on screens tended to show better cognitive processing as teenagers, challenging common assumptions about screen use. Researchers say the key may be balancing physical activity with screen activities that encourage learning, creativity, and active thinking.

mix_items.title: Animals have been eating nature’s original bioplastic for millions of years
mix_items.summary: Nature invented biodegradable plastic long before humans did—and animals may have been feeding on it for hundreds of millions of years. Researchers discovered that dozens of animal species possess enzymes capable of breaking down microbial bioplastics called PHAs, a talent once thought to belong only to microorganisms.

mix_items.title: Chasing Fire Clouds in Utah
mix_items.summary: NASA aircraft are sampling smoke lofted high into the atmosphere by one of the most formidable cloud types in the sky—towering, smoke-infused pyrocumulonimbus. The post Chasing Fire Clouds in Utah appeared first on NASA Science .

mix_items.title: A little-known protein may be fueling Alzheimer’s — and scientists found a way to block it
mix_items.summary: An experimental Alzheimer’s compound prevented damaging protein clumps from forming in the brains of mice, helping nerve cells survive longer and reducing amyloid buildup. The treatment also appeared to improve heart health and slow some signs of aging, raising hopes for an entirely new way to combat dementia.
